idiom_name: ISO date-only keys + readonly version list + valueAt(versions, when)
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds types but no runtime: the realization is a readonly list of versions (or a Map keyed by ISO date strings) with a generic valueAt(versions, when) and a put(versions, from, value) helper, usually wrapped in a small class, where the types are what make it safe - a branded DateOnly type, readonly arrays and as-const literals prevent the two classic mistakes (mutating a Date in place, passing an instant where a calendar date is expected). For the persisted case the pattern usually moves into the database: PostgreSQL range columns or a temporal_tables-style history table queried AS OF a transaction instant, or a hosted change-tracking service such as Bemi over TypeORM whose changes table (primary_key, table, before, after, committed_at) is queried as of a timestamp - both are adapter paths rather than in-language realizations. The TC39 Temporal API is the right Time Point once the runtime ships it; until then ISO-8601 date strings are the safe persisted representation.
pitfalls: ISO date strings compare correctly only if they are exactly YYYY-MM-DD: a stray timestamp ('2024-04-01T00:00:00Z') makes <= disagree with date order, so the type must be validated at the boundary (a schema check) rather than trusted.
readonly is compile-time only: a Date stored in a version can still be mutated at runtime through an alias, so versions should hold strings (or be frozen) rather than Date objects.

Structural typing means a plain string is assignable to a DateOnly alias unless it is branded (string & { readonly __brand: 'DateOnly' }), so the type protects nothing until the brand is applied and only constructible through a parser.

JSON deserialization is untyped at runtime: an empty/missing history array or a null value silently becomes 'no version in force' or a value of the wrong type, so loaded payloads need validation before they reach the accessor.

Numeric dates (Date.getTime(), epoch millis) sort correctly but are instants: using them for a date index reintroduces the time-zone edge, so never mix epoch numbers with ISO day strings in the same history.
